questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: order the verbs of a serial verb construction from the preparatory action to the main action
questions.stem: A speaker wants to say that she took the key and then opened the door, with both verbs taking part in one event. In which sentence do the two verbs stand in the order the construction requires, with nothing joining them?

options.text: 她拿钥匙开门。 (She takes the key and opens the door.)
她开门拿钥匙。 (She opens the door and takes the key.)
options.misconception: believes the main verb has to lead the serial construction

options.text: 她拿钥匙了开门。 (She took the key, and then opened the door.)
options.misconception: closes the first verb with a completion particle inside the serial pair

options.text: 她拿着钥匙开门。 (She is holding the key and opens the door.)
options.misconception: thinks the progressive particle is what links two verbs into one event

questions.explanation: A serial verb construction puts two or more verbs in a single clause with no conjunction and no aspect particle, and they run from the preparatory or incidental action to the main action. questions.stem: One report about a broken window says 有人打碎了玻璃 and a second report says 玻璃被打碎了. What has changed between these two versions of the same event?

options.text: The subject slot now holds the thing that was damaged, so the report is about the damage and not about the doer

options.misconception: believes the passive marker deletes the agent permanently

options.text: The verb has lost its object and is now forbidden from taking a new one
options.misconception: confuses the passive marker with the loss of the verb's object slot

options.text: The sentence can no longer be opened by a time expression placed before the verb
options.misconception: thinks the passive marker blocks the time adverbial slot

questions.learningObjective: choose a clause-final particle that matches the speaker's purpose

Stage two: say which participant each version puts first, and what that changes about what the listener pays attention to.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the first version puts the agent in the subject slot, as in 是小王把我的伞拿走了, which frames the sentence as a piece of news about a person's action. The difference matters because the two versions are not equally useful: one answers how many there are and the other answers how many of what. A learner who has only learned the general word cannot make that second version at all, which is why the error is worth a full two stages rather than a single correction.

Naming the rule is recall, and the two corrected versions are the test of whether the rule is actually usable, because a learner can state the rule and still reach for the same general word every time. Asking what each version asserts, rather than whether it is grammatical, is what stops the repair being a guess.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach how the four kinds of complement are told apart by position
questions.stem: A learner asks how four different kinds of complement are told apart, since each of them follows a verb. Explain what distinguishes a complement of result, a complement of direction, a complement of degree and a potential complement, and why a single position test cannot separate them.

answer.exemplar: The four kinds all stand after a verb, so position alone will not separate them, and that is the honest answer to give first. What separates them is what question each one answers. A complement of result answers what the action produced, as in the sentence about finishing a bowl of rice, and it is closed off so that nothing may be added to its right. A complement of direction answers which way the motion of the verb went, and it is built out of a small fixed inventory of direction words, which is why its two halves have to be in a fixed order when they are combined. A complement of degree answers how the action came out, and it is the only one of the four normally introduced by the marker that also marks necessity, which is where most confusion comes from. A potential complement answers whether the goal of the action could be reached at all, and it is built from the marker plus one of a short set of endings that say the goal was reached, was missed, or could just be managed. The teaching move that works is to make the learner ask which question is being answered, because a learner who does that can classify any new sentence without being told the name of its category, whereas a learner who memorised four lists of words has to be shown the new sentence instead.

questions.explanation: This item asks for a teaching explanation rather than a rule, and the difficulty is that the four categories genuinely overlap in surface order, so a teacher who lists them by position is teaching something false. The exemplar is marked as correct for naming the question each complement answers and for being explicit that one test cannot do the work, which is the point a learner who has memorised lists most needs to hear.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach how a clause-final particle reports the kind of turn the speaker is making
questions.stem: A learner can produce clauses but makes every new sentence sound like a demand. Explain what the clause-final particles contribute, why more than one cannot be used at once, and how a learner can work out which one a situation calls for.

answer.exemplar: The particles that close a clause do not add meaning to what the clause says; they report the kind of turn the speaker is making, and that is why a learner who has all the vocabulary can still sound aggressive. The proposal particle closes a sentence that offers a plan and expects the listener to go along with it. The question particle closes a sentence that wants to know whether something is the case. The sustained-state particle closes a sentence that leaves the listener holding the question of what happens next. The softening particle closes a sentence that asks the listener to bear an unpleasant fact. These are four different social moves built out of one clause each, so a clause can only make one of them at a time, and stacking two is heard as a contradiction rather than as emphasis. The way to work out which one a situation calls for is to ask what the speaker wants to happen next: if the speaker wants agreement, it is a proposal; if the speaker wants information, it is a question; if the speaker wants the listener to supply the next step, it is sustained state. Teaching it as a map of situations rather than as a list of characters is what stops a learner from choosing by which one they remember best.

questions.explanation: The item is marked as a teaching explanation because the failure it targets is not a knowledge gap but a habit, and a habit is not fixed by more rules. The exemplar earns the mark by organising the particles around the speaker's aim and by giving the learner a single diagnostic question, which is the move that survives contact with new sentences.
questions.hint: Ask what the speaker wants the listener to do next, and which particle reports that aim.

questions.learningObjective: teach what the three aspect particles say about the relationship between an event and the moment of speaking

The progressive particle answers the question is the action still under way, and it is the one that belongs on a verb whose state you could photograph, such as keeping something switched on. The completion particle answers the question is the action over, and it is the one that closes the verb phrase, so nothing may be added to the right of it. The experience particle answers the question has this been done at all at some time before, and it reports neither a result nor a continuing state, which is why a sentence carrying it can be followed by more material without difficulty. Because the three answer mutually exclusive questions, one verb phrase can carry only one of them, and a sentence that stacks two of them asks the listener to believe that an event is simultaneously finished and unfinished. That is not a special prohibition, it is what the questions imply, and saying it that way saves a learner from treating the constraint as an arbitrary rule to be memorised one pair at a time.

The exemplar is credited for framing all three particles as answers to questions about one verb, and for deriving the one-per-verb-phrase rule from that framing instead of asserting it, because a learner who has the derivation stops producing stacked markers on their own.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach why moving a time word changes the claim rather than the emphasis
questions.stem: A learner writes the time word in one position in every sentence and is told the sentences are wrong. Explain the two slots a time expression can occupy, what each claims, and how to teach the difference to a learner who thinks moving a word only changes emphasis.

answer.exemplar: The reason the learner is stuck is that moving a time word looks like an editing decision, and in most of the languages they know it is one. Here it is not. A time expression standing in front of the subject frames the whole clause, and everything after it is read under that frame, so a time expression in that slot is a scene-setting device that the rest of the sentence inherits. A time expression standing between the subject and the verb narrows only the action and says nothing about the rest of the clause. A third possibility is to leave a time word loose at the end, which in speech usually means something recent, though no recency is actually asserted. The three placements therefore make three different claims about the same event, and a sentence can be true in one and false in another, which is the test a learner should be given: take a sentence, move the time word into the other slot, and see whether the sentence can still be true. That exercise does more work than a rule, because it makes the learner feel the claim change rather than take the learner's word for it.

questions.explanation: The exemplar earns the mark for insisting that the two slots make different claims rather than different emphases, and for offering a falsification test the learner can run alone. An explanation that only listed the slots would leave the learner with the same habit described in the stem, so the test is the part that matters.
questions.hint: Ask whether a sentence stays true when its time word is moved to the other slot.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach why measure words are chosen by class of thing rather than by frequency
questions.stem: A learner has memorised many nouns and still chooses the wrong measure word every time. Explain what governs the choice, why a general measure word is not a safe default, and how a learner can work out the right word for an unfamiliar noun.

answer.exemplar: The choice is governed by the class of thing the noun names, not by the noun's frequency, and that is why a learner with a large vocabulary does badly on this point: knowing a noun well tells you nothing about its class. Some classes are shape classes, and their measure words follow the shape, so a long thin thing, a flat sheet and a rod each have their own word, and moving a noun from one of these classes to another changes the measure word without changing the noun. Other classes are semantic, including the specific words that are bound to a single noun or a single material and cannot be moved anywhere at all. The general measure word is a fallback, and it is a dangerous one to reach for by habit, because a sentence built on the fallback often carries a count and no information about what is being counted, whereas the specific word says what kind of thing the speaker means. The procedure worth teaching is short: classify the noun before choosing anything, and if the noun is unfamiliar, describe its shape to yourself first. A learner who does that can often get to the right measure word without having met the noun in a counted phrase before, which is exactly the situation in which a memorised list runs out.

questions.explanation: The item targets a habit rather than a gap, and the exemplar is credited for separating the shape classes from the single-noun words and for giving a procedure that works on an unseen noun. An explanation that simply listed the classes would leave the learner no way to act on a noun they have not counted before.
questions.hint: Ask what class of thing the noun names, and what shape it has, before choosing anything.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach that the two markers solve different problems and are not a matched pair
questions.stem: A learner treats the disposal marker and the passive marker as two names for one idea, because a textbook puts them in adjacent chapters. Explain what problem each one solves, why a sentence often needs one rather than the other, and how to break the pairing in a learner's mind.

answer.exemplar: The pairing is a teaching accident and it causes a lot of damage, because the two markers are not opposites and they are not two words for the same operation. The disposal marker solves a word-order problem: an object that is already known to both participants has to be spoken first, and the marker is the device that licenses that and marks the object as the thing being talked about. The passive marker solves a point-of-view problem: it moves a participant out of the subject slot so that a different participant can lead, usually the one that has been acted on. This is why a sentence may need one, the other, both or neither, and why a sentence with both is perfectly normal, as in the sentence about a door being opened by someone, where the marker introduces the known door and the passive marker moves the opener into the background. The way to break the pairing is to give the learner sentences that show the asymmetry directly: put a known object in front of the verb with the disposal marker and no passive marker, and then put an acted-on object in the subject slot with the passive marker and no disposal marker, and ask what changed. In the first the speaker is arranging known material; in the second the speaker is choosing a viewpoint. Those are two different questions, and once a learner has answered them for a pair of sentences, the chapter adjacency stops mattering.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is credited for identifying the false symmetry that the item is built on and for offering a demonstration that breaks it, rather than for restating each marker's function in the abstract. A learner who has seen the asymmetry demonstrated does not need the pairing unmade in words.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two markers solves a word-order problem and which solves a point-of-view problem.
